prompt: What does Microsoft Defender for Cloud's Secure Score represent?
choices: A percentage summarizing adherence to security recommendations
The monthly cost of every Defender plan enabled on the subscription
The count of security incidents currently active in the tenant
The number of subscriptions connected to Defender for Cloud
correctAnswers: A percentage summarizing adherence to security recommendations
explanation: Secure Score is a single percentage summarising how far the environment follows Defender for Cloud recommendations, which is what makes it trendable over time. The incident count is the tempting alternative because it also feels like a security metric, but it measures what is happening to you rather than how well you are configured.

prompt: What does the Defender for Cloud asset Inventory show?
choices: All connected and monitored resources across environments
Only the resources that carry a critical vulnerability today
Only the resources currently reported as non-compliant
Only the virtual machines in the connected subscriptions
correctAnswers: All connected and monitored resources across environments
explanation: Inventory is the full queryable catalogue of monitored resources across Azure, AWS and GCP, not a filtered list. Reading it as "only the non-compliant ones" is the common mistake and it inverts its purpose: you go to Inventory precisely to find the resources nobody has assessed yet.

prompt: Which standard does the free CSPM foundation evaluate configuration against by default?
choices: The Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB)
The PCI-DSS payment card industry standard
The ISO 27001 information security standard
The NIST SP 800-53 control catalog for federal systems
correctAnswers: The Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB)
explanation: The Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark is applied by default and is what Secure Score is computed from. PCI-DSS and ISO 27001 are tempting because they are the standards an auditor names, but they are added on top per scope and never apply on their own.

prompt: Where do you enable additional regulatory standards for a subscription in Defender for Cloud?
choices: Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies
Environment settings ▸ Defender plans for the subscription
Azure Policy ▸ Definitions ▸ Built-in initiatives
Workload protections ▸ Just-in-time VM access
correctAnswers: Regulatory compliance ▸ Manage compliance policies
explanation: Regulatory standards are toggled per scope under Regulatory compliance, in Manage compliance policies. Azure Policy Definitions is the closest miss, because standards are ultimately implemented as policy initiatives — but assigning the initiative by hand does not register the standard in the compliance dashboard.

prompt: When would you add a custom standard in Defender for Cloud?
choices: When no built-in standard matches your internal baseline
When you want to disable the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark
When onboarding an AWS account as a security connector
When enabling a Defender workload protection plan
correctAnswers: When no built-in standard matches your internal baseline
explanation: A custom standard exists for the case where no built-in one matches your internal baseline, so you can assess against your own controls. It does not replace or disable the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, which is the usual assumption: MCSB keeps applying underneath whatever you add.

prompt: Which two non-Azure clouds can be onboarded to Defender for Cloud as connectors?
choices: Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
Alibaba Cloud and DigitalOcean, through a security connector
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and IBM Cloud, jointly
Only AWS is supported, since GCP has no connector at all
correctAnswers: Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
explanation: Defender for Cloud has native multicloud connectors for AWS and GCP, which is what brings their resources into Secure Score and the compliance dashboard. Answering "only AWS" is the dated reading — GCP support followed, and both use the same secret-free federated onboarding rather than stored keys.

prompt: What does Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM) do?
choices: Continuously discovers internet-facing assets from the outside in
Scans the internal virtual machines through an agent installed on each
Manages the certificates held in Azure Key Vault instances
Encrypts data in transit between two peered virtual networks
correctAnswers: Continuously discovers internet-facing assets from the outside in
explanation: EASM discovers internet-facing assets from the outside in, starting from a seed domain, so it finds things you did not know you owned. Agent-based internal scanning is the tempting confusion: an agent can only report on assets you have already onboarded, which is exactly the blind spot EASM exists to cover.

prompt: How does EASM's visibility direction differ from the Defender for Cloud Inventory?
choices: EASM looks from outside in; Inventory looks from inside out
They provide identical visibility over exactly the same asset set
Inventory covers only the AWS and GCP connected accounts
EASM requires an agent installed on every discovered asset
correctAnswers: EASM looks from outside in; Inventory looks from inside out
explanation: The two look in opposite directions and that is the whole distinction: EASM is the attacker view from outside, Inventory is the authenticated view from inside. Treating them as equivalent visibility is the error — an asset nobody onboarded appears in EASM and never in Inventory.

prompt: What is the key distinction between CSPM and CWP in Defender for Cloud?
choices: CSPM is the free posture foundation; CWP is the paid detection
CSPM is the paid tier, whereas CWP comes free of charge with it
They are two names for one and the same feature set
CWP applies only to on-premises servers, never to Azure
correctAnswers: CSPM is the free posture foundation; CWP is the paid detection
explanation: CSPM is the free posture layer that answers "are we configured securely?"; CWP is the set of paid plans that answer "is something attacking us now?". Reversing the two is the classic slip, and it matters commercially: enabling a Defender plan is a billing decision, whereas reviewing Secure Score costs nothing.

prompt: What is the relationship between MCSB and additional regulatory standards like ISO 27001?
choices: MCSB is the default baseline; other standards layer on top
Enabling ISO 27001 disables MCSB across the whole subscription
Only one standard can be active on a subscription at once
MCSB and ISO 27001 cannot be assigned to the same scope
correctAnswers: MCSB is the default baseline; other standards layer on top
explanation: MCSB is always applied and additional standards layer on top of it, so several can be active at once. Believing that enabling ISO 27001 disables MCSB is the trap: Secure Score would appear to change for no reason, when in fact nothing was replaced.

prompt: Which Defender for Cloud view shows pass/fail status per individual regulatory control?
choices: The Regulatory compliance dashboard
The Secure Score tile on its own
The Workload protections overview
The asset Inventory blade on its own
correctAnswers: The Regulatory compliance dashboard
explanation: The Regulatory compliance dashboard maps each enabled standard to its controls and shows pass or fail per control. The Secure Score tile is the tempting answer because it is the headline number, but it aggregates everything into one percentage and cannot tell you which control failed.

prompt: Why onboard an AWS account into Defender for Cloud?
choices: To extend Secure Score and compliance visibility to AWS
Because it is required before enabling any Azure Defender plan
To migrate the AWS workloads into Azure automatically
To replace AWS IAM with Azure role-based access control
correctAnswers: To extend Secure Score and compliance visibility to AWS
explanation: Onboarding AWS extends the same Secure Score and compliance view to it, so one dashboard covers both clouds. It neither migrates workloads nor replaces AWS IAM, which is the misreading that makes teams hesitate: the connector reads posture, it does not take over the account.

prompt: During an acquisition, why would a security team run Defender EASM against the target company?
choices: To surface unknown or shadow-IT internet-facing assets first
To automatically patch every vulnerability it happens to discover
To enable Transparent Data Encryption on their databases
To assign Azure RBAC roles to the acquired company staff
correctAnswers: To surface unknown or shadow-IT internet-facing assets first
explanation: EASM surfaces unknown, forgotten and shadow-IT assets before an attacker does, which is why it fits acquisition due diligence — you cannot inventory what you have not been told about. It discovers rather than remediates, so expecting it to patch what it finds is the wrong model.

prompt: Secure Score is dropping. Which action would most directly raise it?
choices: Remediating the recommendations that carry the most weight
Enabling more of the Defender workload protection plans instead
Adding another regulatory standard to the subscription
Running an External Attack Surface Management scan
correctAnswers: Remediating the recommendations that carry the most weight
explanation: Secure Score reflects adherence to recommendations; remediating high-impact recommendations raises it. The other actions add coverage/standards but don't directly raise the score by themselves.

prompt: Which capability is part of the FREE CSPM foundation rather than a paid plan?
choices: Secure Score and its security recommendations
Agentless vulnerability scanning of the VM disks
Defender for Servers endpoint detection
Defender for Storage malware detection
correctAnswers: Secure Score and its security recommendations
explanation: Secure Score, recommendations, inventory and MCSB assessment are the free foundational CSPM layer. Agentless vulnerability scanning is the closest miss and the one people assume is free because it needs no deployment, but it belongs to the paid Defender for Servers plan.

prompt: A team assumes enabling PCI-DSS in Defender for Cloud will replace the default benchmark. What is correct?
choices: MCSB remains applied; PCI-DSS is added alongside it
MCSB applies only to AWS, so PCI-DSS replaces it here
PCI-DSS overrides and disables MCSB on the scope
Only the PCI-DSS controls are evaluated afterwards
correctAnswers: MCSB remains applied; PCI-DSS is added alongside it
explanation: Standards are additive: MCSB stays applied and PCI-DSS is assessed alongside it. Expecting PCI-DSS to override is the assumption worth breaking, because a team that believes it will stop watching MCSB findings that never went away.

prompt: Which tool answers the question 'What internet-facing assets do we have that we might not know about?'
choices: Microsoft Defender EASM
The compliance dashboard
Just-in-time VM access
The Secure Score tile
correctAnswers: Microsoft Defender EASM
explanation: Only EASM answers a question about assets you might not know you have, because it works from the outside in. Secure Score and the compliance dashboard both assess resources already connected, so neither can reveal something that was never onboarded.

prompt: Which best describes the role of the asset Inventory in security operations?
choices: A queryable catalog of resources and their security posture
A list of only the alerts raised in the last twenty-four hours
The billing breakdown of the enabled Defender plans
A record of every user sign-in across the tenant
correctAnswers: A queryable catalog of resources and their security posture
explanation: Inventory is a queryable catalogue of resources with their posture context, backed by Azure Resource Graph, which is what lets one query span three clouds. Reading it as an alert list is the confusion to avoid: it catalogues what exists rather than what just happened, and alerts have their own lifecycle on the workload-protection side.

prompt: A CISO wants one compliance view spanning Azure, AWS, and GCP. What must be in place?
choices: Multicloud connectors for AWS and GCP in Defender for Cloud
A separate Microsoft Sentinel workspace for each of the clouds
An External Attack Surface Management scan of each cloud
A resource lock applied to each connected subscription
correctAnswers: Multicloud connectors for AWS and GCP in Defender for Cloud
explanation: One compliance view across three clouds requires the AWS and GCP connectors, because a resource has to be connected before it can be assessed. A separate Sentinel workspace per cloud is the tempting alternative, but Sentinel is for events rather than posture and would give three views instead of one.

prompt: Which statement about CSPM vs CWP is FALSE?
choices: CWP is the free foundation and CSPM the paid plans
CSPM includes Secure Score and its recommendation list
CSPM focuses on configuration and security posture
CWP focuses on active threat detection at runtime
correctAnswers: CWP is the free foundation and CSPM the paid plans
explanation: The false statement inverts the two: CSPM is the free foundation, whereas CWP is the set of paid plans. Everything else listed is true, which is what makes the reversal easy to miss on a quick read — the sentence is well formed and only the two labels are swapped.

prompt: Which activity is squarely CSPM (posture), not CWP (threat protection)?
choices: Remediating a recommendation to encrypt a storage account
Responding to an alert about anomalous access to storage data
Investigating an endpoint detection finding on a VM
Triaging an alert about a malware upload to a blob
correctAnswers: Remediating a recommendation to encrypt a storage account
explanation: Acting on a configuration recommendation is posture work, so it is CSPM. The three alert-driven activities are tempting because they are all security operations, but each starts from a detection rather than from a misconfiguration — that is the line between the two halves of the product.

prompt: What does 'assess compliance against a security framework' mean in Defender for Cloud?
choices: Mapping configuration to a standard's controls, pass or fail
Blocking any deployment that would violate the standard at all
Automatically remediating every control that has failed
Encrypting the data at rest in order to meet the standard
correctAnswers: Mapping configuration to a standard's controls, pass or fail
explanation: Assessing compliance means mapping configuration to a standard's controls and reporting pass or fail. It does not block deployments and does not remediate, which is the expectation to correct: enforcement is Azure Policy's Deny effect, and remediation needs a remediation task.

prompt: Which is NOT something the free CSPM foundation provides?
choices: Endpoint detection and response on servers
Secure Score across the whole of the subscription
The security recommendations list
The asset inventory across clouds
correctAnswers: Endpoint detection and response on servers
explanation: Endpoint detection and response comes with the paid Defender for Servers plan, not with free CSPM. Secure Score, recommendations and inventory are all free, which is why EDR is the one to recognise here — it is the only capability in the list that requires a plan to be enabled.

prompt: A resource keeps failing a control in the regulatory compliance dashboard. What is the intended remediation path?
choices: Follow the linked recommendation to fix the configuration
Disable the resource inside the Defender for Cloud inventory blade
Remove the standard so the failing control disappears
Ignore it, since compliance reporting is informational
correctAnswers: Follow the linked recommendation to fix the configuration
explanation: Each control maps to assessments and recommendations you remediate to raise compliance, so the fix is upstream in the configuration. Removing the standard is the tempting shortcut and it is the wrong instinct: the control disappears from the dashboard while the underlying weakness stays exactly where it was.

prompt: Which two are part of the free CSPM foundation? (Choose two.)
choices: Secure Score for the subscription
The asset inventory across clouds
Defender for Storage malware detection
Agentless vulnerability scanning of disks
correctAnswers: Secure Score for the subscription
The asset inventory across clouds
explanation: Secure Score and asset inventory are free foundational CSPM. Malware detection and agentless scanning are the tempting pair because neither requires deploying anything, but both belong to paid workload-protection plans.

prompt: Which two statements about compliance standards in Microsoft Defender for Cloud are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: The Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark applies by default
Custom standards can be added when built-in ones do not fit
Enabling PCI-DSS replaces the default benchmark on the scope
Only one standard can be active on a subscription at once
correctAnswers: The Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark applies by default
Custom standards can be added when built-in ones do not fit
explanation: MCSB is applied by default and custom standards exist for baselines the built-ins do not cover. Neither distractor holds: standards are additive rather than exclusive, so PCI-DSS does not replace MCSB and more than one can be active on a subscription.

prompt: Which two directions of visibility do Inventory and EASM respectively represent? (Choose two.)
choices: Inventory is inside-out, the authenticated admin view
EASM is outside-in, the attacker view of public assets
Inventory is outside-in only, like an attacker would see
EASM needs an agent installed on every internal machine
correctAnswers: Inventory is inside-out, the authenticated admin view
EASM is outside-in, the attacker view of public assets
explanation: Inventory is the inside-out authenticated catalogue and EASM is the outside-in attacker view. The distractors invert the direction and invent an agent requirement — EASM is agentless by construction, since it looks at assets you may not control.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (one score summarizing configuration compliance across Azure, an AWS account, and a GCP project), what should Adatum configure?
choices: Onboard AWS and GCP as connectors in Defender for Cloud
Enable External Attack Surface Management, and nothing else
Compile separate reports from each cloud's native tools
Migrate the AWS and GCP workloads into Azure first
correctAnswers: Onboard AWS and GCP as connectors in Defender for Cloud
explanation: One score across three clouds needs the AWS and GCP connectors, because Secure Score only covers connected environments. Compiling separate reports from each cloud's native tools is the tempting workaround and it fails the requirement: three numbers is not one score.

prompt: Referring to requirement 4 (discover a subsidiary's internet-facing web servers the way an attacker would), which tool should Adatum use?
choices: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management
The Defender for Cloud asset inventory blade on its own
The Azure Policy compliance dashboard for that scope
Defender for Servers agentless disk scanning, alone
correctAnswers: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management
explanation: Discovering a subsidiary's internet-facing servers without their cooperation is outside-in work, which is EASM. Inventory is the closest miss but it only sees resources already connected, so it cannot find assets nobody has told you about.

prompt: Adatum's leadership asks for a single number to track whether the environment's security configuration is improving over time. Which Defender for Cloud metric fits?
choices: Secure Score over time
Regulatory standards enabled
EASM-discovered assets
Enabled Defender plans
correctAnswers: Secure Score over time
explanation: Secure Score is the single percentage designed to be trended. The count of enabled Defender plans is the tempting proxy because it rises as you invest, but it measures coverage purchased rather than configuration improved — you can enable every plan and fix nothing.

prompt: Order the steps to get one unified compliance view across Azure, AWS, and GCP.
reorderItems: Onboard the AWS account as a multicloud connector in Defender for Cloud
Onboard the GCP project as a multicloud connector
Review the unified Secure Score and Inventory across all three
Enable a regulatory standard (e.g. ISO 27001) across the connected environments
explanation: Both clouds must be connected before any unified view exists, so the connectors come first and the review comes after. Additional standards are layered last, since a standard assessed against an unconnected environment reports nothing rather than failing visibly.

prompt: Order the steps to discover a newly acquired subsidiary's unknown internet-facing assets before onboarding it.
reorderItems: Run a Microsoft Defender EASM discovery scan against the subsidiary's known domains
Review the discovered inventory of internet-facing assets
Investigate any unexpected or shadow-IT assets found
Bring the subsidiary's known Azure resources into Defender for Cloud's inventory
explanation: External discovery comes first, because the point is to find assets nobody listed; investigation follows, and only then are the confirmed resources onboarded for inside-out monitoring. Starting from onboarding is the instinct to resist, since it cannot reach anything you do not already know about.

prompt: Configure this simplified Defender for Cloud environment settings screen to extend posture management to a connected AWS account.
explanation: An AWS connector onboards the account, and MCSB is the default benchmark applied to assess it exactly as it does for Azure resources. Expecting to have to choose a standard manually is the misconception: nothing needs enabling for MCSB to apply, whereas PCI-DSS or ISO 27001 would.

prompt: Proposed solution: Track the number of Defender plans enabled each month. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Counting enabled plans measures how much coverage has been bought, not whether the configuration behind it improved. It is the tempting metric because it goes up and is easy to report, but it can rise while Secure Score falls.

prompt: Proposed solution: Track Secure Score over time in Defender for Cloud. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: Secure Score is precisely the single percentage that trends configuration quality across connected environments, which is what the requirement asks for. Note the constraint it carries: it only covers environments that are connected, so an unonboarded cloud silently does not count.

prompt: Proposed solution: Track the number of EASM-discovered assets each month. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: The EASM asset count measures the size of the external attack surface, not the quality of the configuration. It is a useful number, but it can grow simply because discovery improved — so it cannot be read as posture getting worse or better.

prompt: Which command lists, for each resource type, whether the Defender plan is on the Free (CSPM only) or Standard (CWP) tier?
choices: az security pricing list
az security score list
az defender plan list
az security assessment tiers
correctAnswers: az security pricing list
explanation: Defender plan tiers are exposed as 'pricings' — `az security pricing list` / Get-AzSecurityPricing. The other subcommands don't exist.

prompt: Which command queries all storage accounts across subscriptions at scale, the way the Defender for Cloud inventory does?
choices: az graph query, projecting name and location from Resources
az resource list with a type filter across all subscriptions
az storage account list with all tenants included
az security inventory list filtered by resource type
correctAnswers: az graph query, projecting name and location from Resources
explanation: Azure Resource Graph (`az graph query`, KQL) is the at-scale query engine behind the inventory. `az resource list` is per-subscription and slower; the other two don't exist.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet runs an Azure Resource Graph KQL query?
choices: Search-AzGraph
Invoke-AzResourceQuery
Get-AzResourceGraph
Query-AzInventory
correctAnswers: Search-AzGraph
explanation: Search-AzGraph, from the Az.ResourceGraph module, is the cmdlet that runs a KQL query against Resource Graph. The other three do not exist, which is the real lesson here: plausible-looking cmdlet names are how these items catch you, so recognise the module rather than guess the verb.

prompt: In `az security pricing list` output, what does tier 'Free' mean for a resource type?
choices: Only the free CSPM foundation applies to that resource type
The paid plan is active but discounted for that resource type
The resource type is excluded from Secure Score entirely
Agentless scanning is enabled for it at no cost at all
correctAnswers: Only the free CSPM foundation applies to that resource type
explanation: Free means the posture layer only — recommendations and Secure Score — with no workload threat detection for that resource type; Standard is the paid plan. Reading Free as "excluded from Secure Score" is the trap: posture coverage is independent of tier, so a Free resource type is still scored, just not defended.

prompt: Where in the CLI/portal flow are AWS and GCP environments connected to Defender for Cloud?
choices: Environment settings ▸ Add environment
az security pricing create --tier Standard
az graph query with the AWS provider
Azure Arc ▸ Servers ▸ Add a machine
correctAnswers: Environment settings ▸ Add environment
explanation: Multicloud onboarding creates a security connector under Environment settings. `security pricing` sets plan tiers (there is no 'AWS' pricing name); Arc onboards individual machines, not cloud accounts.
